verses.1: Al-Mizan treats the verses as an oath. It defines al-ḍuḥā as spreading sunlight and the stretching day, hence the forenoon, and sajw as the night's stillness under darkness.
verses.2: Al-Mizan treats the verses as an oath. It defines al-ḍuḥā as spreading sunlight and the stretching day, hence the forenoon, and sajw as the night's stillness under darkness.
verses.3: Al-Mizan defines tawdīʿ as abandonment, leaving, or forsaking, and qilā as dislike or intense dislike. The reassurance is the crux of the preceding oaths and is related to the interruption of revelation through their day-and-night imagery.
verses.4: Al-Mizan reads the verse as extending the assurance of divine grace and honor: the Prophet's present life is under God's grace and mercy, but his life in the hereafter will be better still.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says the verse confirms the preceding promise: neither God's gift nor the Prophet's satisfaction is qualified, so it signifies an unconditional gift and absolute satisfaction. Some exegetes extend it to this life as well as the hereafter.
verses.6: Al-Mizan treats the verse as recalling God's blessings on the Prophet: his father died before his birth, his mother when he was two, and his guardian-grandfather when he was eight, after which his uncle raised him. It also reports an interpretation of yatīm as peerless or matchless, under which God gathered people around the uniquely incomparable Prophet.
verses.7: Al-Mizan takes ḍalāl here as being devoid of divine guidance: no human finds it independently, though God's grace was entwined with the Prophet from his creation. It regards lack of knowledge as a close reading, but reports as weak the view that he was unrecognized among people and the accounts that he was literally lost in childhood or on journeys. The verse thus concerns guidance in the prophetic sense, not moral error.
verses.8: Al-Mizan glosses ʿāʾil as one without wealth and recalls that the Prophet had been poor before God enriched him through marriage to the wealthy Khadījah b. Khuwaylid, who offered him her wealth. Some exegetes instead take being made free from need as having prayers answered.
verses.9: Al-Mizan explains qahr as domination and humiliation together, though it may also denote either one separately; the command therefore forbids belittling the orphan.
verses.10: Al-Mizan glosses nahr as roughly repulsing and turning someone away; the command forbids such harsh dismissal of the beggar.
verses.11: Al-Mizan says proclaiming a blessing may mean speaking of it or showing it in action, and is therefore gratitude. Although addressed to the Prophet, the commands concerning the orphan, seeker, and blessings are universal and arise from his own remembered experiences: do not humiliate an orphan or harm the orphan's property, do not turn away one seeking guidance or provision, and manifest rather than conceal the Lord's generosity, grace, and mercy.
